title: Before your next discovery call
text:
Most first calls with a prospect go wrong in the first five minutes. We start talking about features, and the customer politely waits for the call to end. This quarter, let's try something different: the customer should do most of the talking.

Open with a simple request: walk me through your current process. Then listen. Ask how many people touch an invoice before it is paid, and find out where documents get stuck. Keep your questions open. Instead of asking whether they use shared drives, ask them how they find a contract today.

Two questions tell you more than any others. The first is about timing: What's prompting you to look at this now? A new regulation, a failed audit, or a new CFO usually means there is real pressure. The second is about the goal: What would success look like for you? If they can't answer, the project probably has no budget yet.

Before you hang up, summarize what you heard. Start with So if I'm hearing you correctly, and repeat their three main problems in their own words. Finally, don't forget to ask who else is involved in the decision. Deals rarely die because of price. They die because we never met the person who signs.

title: How I explained my job to my neighbor
text:
Last week, my neighbor asked me what I actually do. I sell cloud software for documents, I said, and I watched him lose interest. So I tried again, without any technical words.

In a nutshell, we help companies find the right document in seconds instead of digging through folders. Think about a mid-sized manufacturer. Invoices arrive by email, contracts sit in three different places, and nobody knows which version is the latest. What that means for you is simple: less time searching, fewer mistakes, and no panic when the auditor calls.

The key idea is a single source of truth. Every contract, invoice, and delivery note lives in one place, with a clear history of who changed what. Access is controlled, so people only see what they need.

My neighbor nodded. Then he asked the question every customer asks: how long does it take to get started? That is where the cloud really helps. There is no server to install, and the team can work with the system from day one.

He still doesn't find my job exciting. But for the first time, he understood it.

title: Your question about the price
text:
Subject: Your question about the price

Dear Ms. Keller,

Thank you for your time on Tuesday. You mentioned that our offer is higher than the quote from your current provider. I understand it may seem high at first glance, so I would like to put the numbers into context.

Your team currently spends roughly a third of its week searching for invoices and contracts. Based on the figures you shared, that is about 1,400 hours per year. If our system cuts that time in half, it should save you around 60,000 euros a year.

When we look at the total cost of ownership, the picture changes. Your current solution needs its own servers, regular updates, and an external consultant for every change. Our price already includes hosting, updates, and support. Over a three-year period, we estimate that your costs would be about 15 percent lower, even though the license itself is more expensive.

In similar projects, the system usually pays for itself within 18 months. Of course, every company is different, so I would suggest a short pilot with your accounts payable team. That way, you can check the numbers with your own data before you commit.

Best regards

title: Answers to your security questions
text:
Subject: Answers to your security questions

Hi Mr. Brandt,

Thanks again for the detailed list of questions. Here are the answers our security team and I can give you today.

All customer data is hosted in EU data centers in Frankfurt and Amsterdam. No data is transferred outside the EU, and our subcontractors are listed in the data processing agreement. Documents are encrypted at rest and in transit, and the keys are managed separately from the storage.

Access is controlled by role-based access. Your administrators decide which groups can see, edit, or delete documents, and every action is logged. For tax-relevant records, we offer audit-proof archiving in line with GoBD. Once a document has been archived, it cannot be changed or deleted before the retention period ends.

You also asked about backups. Backups are created every night and are stored in a second data center. In the unlikely case of an outage, your data can be restored within four hours.

One question I can't answer with certainty yet: whether our certificate covers the new AI search module. Let me double-check that and get back to you by Friday. I would rather give you a precise answer than a quick one.

Best regards

title: E-invoicing in Germany: why waiting is the expensive option
text:
E-invoicing in Germany: why waiting is the expensive option

As of January 1, 2025, every German company must be able to receive electronic invoices. For sending, the mandate is being phased in: larger companies will have to issue e-invoices from 2027, and smaller ones from 2028. On top of that, the EU is preparing its ViDA package, which is going to connect invoices with digital tax reporting.

Many managing directors are still waiting. Their logic sounds reasonable: the deadline is still some time away, and the software market is changing. But for most companies, it's not a question of if, but when. And the later they start, the more expensive the project gets, because consultants and IT partners will be fully booked at the end of 2026 and in 2027.

Companies that get ahead of the deadline have a clear advantage. They can test the process with a few suppliers, train their accounting team, and fix problems while volumes are still low. At the same time, they start saving money right away, because digital invoices are processed faster and with fewer errors.

The message for decision makers is simple. The rules will not go away. The question is whether you want to stay compliant under pressure or on your own schedule.

title: Three slides for the board
text:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for making time for this. Let me walk you through three slides, and then we'll have plenty of time for questions.

The first slide shows where your documents are today. Right now, your teams work with four different systems. What really matters here is not the number of systems, but the time people lose switching between them.

This brings me to the second slide. The chart shows the number of invoices that our customer Hartmann Foods processed digitally over the last two years. In the first quarter, it was around 20,000 invoices. By the end of last year, the number had more than doubled, to 45,000, while the team stayed the same size. It was automation, not extra staff, that made the difference.

On the third slide, you can see the plan for your company: a pilot in accounting, then purchasing, then HR. The total investment is 2.5 million euros over five years.

Yes, Mr. Weber? You're asking about the integration with your ERP system. That's a great question, and I'll come back to that in a minute, because it is exactly what the pilot is designed to test.

title: Notes from today’s negotiation
text:
Subject: Notes from today's negotiation with Lindner Group

Team,

Here is a short summary of today's call with Ms. Roth from procurement. She opened with a clear demand: a 20 percent discount, or they would stay with their current provider. I didn't react to the number right away. Instead, I asked: Where do you have some flexibility? It turned out that the budget is fixed for this year, but the contract length is open.

That gave us room to move. I told her: If you could commit to three years, we could offer a lower price per user. We also discussed payment terms. She asked for 90 days, which we normally don't accept. I said, That's not something I can agree to today, but I will check it with our finance team.

In the end, we agreed on 10 percent for a three-year contract, with the option to add more users at the same price. The question of the setup fee is still open. We decided to park it and discuss it next week.

If finance approves the payment terms, we should be able to sign before the end of the quarter.

Best

title: Partnership idea for Brightline IT

Subject: Partnership idea for Brightline IT

We met briefly at the partner event in Manchester last month, where you mentioned that many of your clients are asking about document management in the cloud. I've been thinking about our conversation, and I believe there could be a mutually beneficial partnership between our companies.

Your team already manages the IT of more than 200 mid-sized companies. If you added our platform to your portfolio, you could offer those clients a complete solution for invoices, contracts, and archiving. What's in it for you is recurring revenue: partners earn a commission of 20 percent on every license, every year, as long as the customer stays.

We would not leave you alone with the product. Our program includes enablement and co-marketing, which means technical training for your consultants, ready-made campaigns, and joint events with our sales team. If a project were too big for your team, our experts would support you on site.

I realize you probably receive offers like this every week, so I will keep it short. Would you be open to a quick call next Tuesday or Wednesday? Twenty minutes would be enough to see whether it makes sense for both sides.

title: Delay in your migration project
text:
Subject: Delay in your migration project

Dear Mr. Schulz,

First of all, I owe you an apology. We promised that your old archive would be fully migrated by September 15, and we have missed that date. I know your team has been waiting for almost two weeks, and I understand how frustrating that is.

Here is where we stand. We've identified the root cause: about 80,000 of your older files use a format that our import tool did not recognize. Our engineers have already converted half of them, and they have tested the rest on a smaller sample. So far, no data has been lost.

Here's what we're doing about it. Two additional engineers have joined the project this week, and they are working on the remaining files every day. We expect the migration to be complete by October 2. Until then, your team can still access all documents in the old system.

To make up for it, we will not charge you for the extra migration work, and we will extend your support package by three months at no cost.

I'll keep you posted with a short update every Friday. If you would like to discuss this by phone, I'm available anytime this week.

Best regards

title: Thirty minutes of pipeline review
text:
Every Monday at nine, I run a 30-minute pipeline review with my team. Last week, it almost got out of control.

Let's get started, I said at 9:02, and shared the forecast. We had 14 open deals worth 1.8 million euros, and six of them were due to close by the end of the quarter on September 30. I asked each account manager for a one-sentence update.

Julia began, but after two minutes she was still talking about a customer's new office building. Can I just jump in here? I asked. What's the next step, and when is it? She laughed and said: a demo on Thursday at 2 p.m.

Then Tobias started a long discussion about our price list for public sector customers. It's an important topic, but not for this meeting. Let's take that offline, I suggested, and we scheduled a separate call for Wednesday.

Near the end, we found a problem: nobody had followed up with a prospect in Vienna for three weeks. Who's going to own this? Tobias volunteered and promised to call them by Tuesday noon.

To wrap up, I summarized the three action items, with names and dates. We finished at 9:29, one minute early.

title: Five minutes at the booth
text:
It's the second day of the trade show in Stuttgart, and our booth is busy. A man in a gray jacket is looking at our poster about e-invoicing, so I walk over and say hello. What brings you to the show? He tells me he works for a logistics company near Hamburg and is looking for ideas for their archive.

I ask him a follow-up question: How's business on your end? He laughs and says they are hiring right now, because two big customers are moving their warehouses to northern Germany. That explains his visit: more customers mean more paper.

We talk for about five minutes. I don't pitch the product. Instead, I ask how they handle delivery notes today, and I tell him a short story about a customer with the same problem. Then I notice that his colleague is waving at him from the next booth. I'll let you get back to it, I say, and we exchange cards.

The next morning, I send him a LinkedIn message: Great connecting with you at the trade show in Stuttgart. Here is the case study I mentioned. Let's stay in touch. Two weeks later, he asks for a demo.

title: Polite but firm
text:
The trip to the trade show in Chicago started badly. My flight from Frankfurt was two hours late, so I missed my connection in New York. At the transfer desk, I stayed calm and asked: Could you rebook me on the next flight? The agent typed for a long time and finally found a seat on an evening flight.

When I arrived at the hotel close to midnight, the receptionist gave me a small room next to the elevator. That's not what I booked, I told her politely. I had reserved a quiet room with a desk, because I needed to prepare a presentation. She checked her screen. There must have been a mix-up with the booking system, she said. The hotel couldn't have lost my reservation, because I had the confirmation on my phone.

I was tired, but I didn't raise my voice. I was wondering if there's anything you could do tonight, I said. I'd appreciate it if you could at least move me tomorrow morning. Ten minutes later, she handed me a new key: a corner room on the twelfth floor, with a desk and a view of the lake.

The lesson? Polite but firm works better than angry.

title: The shortcut
text:
Last spring, my friend Tom and I had planned a weekend in the mountains. We had booked a small cabin, packed the car, and left early on Saturday morning. Everything was going well until the GPS sent us up a narrow forest road.

So there I was, in a rented minivan, on a muddy road with no cell phone signal and a very hungry friend next to me. It was getting dark, and I had no idea where we were. After twenty minutes, we saw a farmer who was fixing a fence. I explained our problem, and he laughed.

It turned out that we had driven past the cabin an hour earlier. The owner had changed the address online, but our GPS was still using the old map. The farmer drove ahead of us with his tractor all the way back to the main road.

The funny thing is, Tom still says it was the best part of the trip. Long story short, we arrived late, ate cold pizza, and slept like logs. In the end, the weekend turned out perfect, and now I always download offline maps before a trip.

q.de: Warum hat das Navi sie falsch geleitet?
q.en: Why did the GPS send them the wrong way?

options: It was still using the old map.
core.quote: our GPS was still using the old map

why.de: Der Besitzer hatte die Adresse geändert, das Navi kannte nur die alte Karte.
why.en: The owner had changed the address, but the GPS only knew the old map.

q.de: Wie sieht der Autor die Reise heute?
q.en: How does the writer see the trip today?

options: As a reason to be angry at the farmer
between.quote: In the end, the weekend turned out perfect

why.de: Er erzählt mit Humor und sagt, dass das Wochenende am Ende perfekt war.
why.en: He tells the story with humor and says the weekend turned out perfect in the end.

title: Will AI replace salespeople?
text:
At lunch today, my colleague Mark claimed that AI will replace most sales jobs within five years. He had just read an article about chatbots that can write offers and answer customer questions on their own.

I see where you're coming from, but I don't think it's that simple, I said. I'd argue that AI will probably change the job more than it replaces it. Tools that summarize calls or draft emails are already saving us time. But a customer who is about to spend half a million euros still wants to talk to a person they trust.

Mark wasn't convinced. Customers don't care who writes the offer, he said, as long as it's fast and cheap. That's a fair point for small, simple deals, I admitted. If you only sell a few licenses, a website and a chatbot might be enough.

It's a bit more nuanced than that for complex projects, though. Someone has to understand the politics inside a company, notice when the CFO is nervous, and find a compromise that works for everyone. At least for now, that is hard to automate.

In the end, we agreed on one thing: salespeople who use AI well will likely replace those who don't. Whether Mark is right about the rest, time will tell.

q.en: What does Mark believe?

title: Heating problem in apartment 4B
text:
Subject: Heating problem in apartment 4B

Dear Mr. Novak,

I'm writing because I've been having trouble with the heating in my apartment. The radiator in the living room, the one that is next to the balcony door, only gets warm for about an hour in the morning. After that, it stays cold, even when I turn it up all the way.

It's been going on for about a week, and the nights are getting colder. I also noticed a small leak at the pipe that connects the radiator to the wall. There is a little water on the floor every morning, and I'm worried that it will damage the wooden floor.

Could you take a look at it, or send someone who can repair it? I work from home on Mondays and Fridays, so those days would be best for me. Would it be possible to arrange a visit before the weekend?

If the repair takes longer, what are my options? My neighbor told me that tenants can sometimes pay less rent while the heating doesn't work, but I would much rather have the problem fixed.

Thank you in advance for your help.

Best regards

q.en: What is the main problem?

why.en: The radiator only gets warm for an hour in the morning and stays cold after that.
